set.title: Mock 15
set.desc: Real vignettes never used before plus the Econ growth vignette you missed (names and numbers changed), 44 questions, 11 vignettes, 2 h 12 min

vignettes.body:
Han Seung-woo is an equity analyst with Daegu Securities. Han is writing a research report on HanSol Electronics, a South Korean company that is dual-listed on a US exchange and complies with US GAAP. As part of his analysis, Han wants to determine the intrinsic value of HanSol's common shares under both residual income and comparable valuation methods.
To support the valuation process, Han assembles in Exhibit 1 selected financial information from HanSol's 2013 and 2012 audited financial statements (values stated in South Korean won [KRW]). Other financial data pertaining to the valuation of HanSol's shares at 31 December 2013 are shown in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 1: Selected Information from HanSol's 2013 and 2012 Financial Statements (KRW millions, except where noted)
# Item | 2013 | 2012
Net income | 96,000 |
Dividends | 38,400 |
Number of common shares outstanding (actual) | 30,000,000 |
Total stockholders' equity at 31 December | 720,000 | 660,000

Exhibit 2: Other Financial Data for HanSol Electronics
Required return on equity | 10%
Market price per share at 31 December 2013 | KRW58,000

At 31 December 2013, Han provided the following forecasted fundamentals for HanSol:
*  expected long-term return on equity (ROE) is 13%; and
*  after 2014, earnings and dividends will grow at 6% per year.
Han's supervisor is concerned that the residual income model may not apply, and she asks Han to investigate possible clean surplus violations. Looking at HanSol's financial statement information, Han considers three items with possible violations to clean surplus accounting:
Item 1: Non-domestic currency translation adjustments from the consolidation of any self-sustaining subsidiary companies (for which the local currency is the functional currency)
Item 2: Marketable securities classified as available-for-sale
Item 3: Non-domestic currency transactions with customers and suppliers
Upon completing the analysis, Han concludes that the net effects are not material to the financial statements and, accordingly, makes no adjustments to the information in Exhibit 1.
In a recent conference call, HanSol's management presented its plan to improve future profitability, particularly the economic value added (EVA), by focusing on the following three strategic company goals:
Goal 1: Reduce research and development (R&D) expenses.
Goal 2: Adjust financial leverage to the optimal level.
Goal 3: Implement efficiencies in administrative functions.

questions.q: Using the information in Exhibits 1 and 2, HanSol's residual income (in KRW millions) in 2013 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. This calculates the equity charge on end-of-year equity: 96,000 − (0.10 × 720,000) = 24,000.
B. Correct. Residual income = net income − equity charge based on start-of-year equity: 96,000 − (0.10 × 660,000) = KRW30,000 million.
C. Incorrect. This ignores the equity charge: net income − dividends = 96,000 − 38,400 = 57,600.

questions.q: Using the information in Exhibits 1 and 2, Han's forecasts, and the single-stage (constant growth) residual income approach, the justified price-to-book ratio (P/B) at 31 December 2013 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Justified P/B = (ROE − g) ÷ (r − g) = (0.13 − 0.06) ÷ (0.10 − 0.06) = 1.75.
B. Incorrect. This uses the historical 2013 ROE (96,000 ÷ 720,000 = 13.33%) instead of the expected long-term ROE of 13%.
C. Incorrect. This is the market price divided by book value per share: 58,000 ÷ (720,000 ÷ 30) = 2.42.

questions.q: With respect to the three items that Han examined, which item is least likely to result in a clean surplus accounting violation?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Translation adjustments of self-sustaining subsidiaries bypass the income statement and go to other comprehensive income, which violates clean surplus.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Unrealized gains and losses on available-for-sale securities bypass the income statement and go to other comprehensive income, which violates clean surplus.
C. Correct. Correct. Foreign currency transactions with customers and suppliers are accounted for in both the income statement and balance sheet at fair value, so they do not violate clean surplus accounting.

questions.q: Which of management's three strategic goals will least likely result in a higher EVA for HanSol?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Adjusting financial leverage to the optimal level lowers the cost of capital and raises EVA.
B. Correct. Correct. R&D costs are added back to NOPAT when calculating EVA, so cutting R&D lowers NOPAT and EVA.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. Administrative efficiencies lower operating expenses, raise NOPAT and raise EVA.

vignettes.body:
Nadia Kovacs is an activist investor with Valdor Partners. Valdor recently acquired a 9.9% equity position in Brenta Corporation and is seeking two board seats.
Brenta is a mature company that has maintained a constant dividend payout ratio and does not currently have a share repurchase program. In public comments, Kovacs recommends a material increase in Brenta's dividend payout ratio and benchmarking the payout to Brenta's competitors.
Kovacs tells Brenta's management that Torvik, one of Brenta's competitors, has a 60% target payout ratio with an adjustment period of five years. Torvik's most recent annual dividend was $0.40 per share. Torvik's EPS is expected to be $2.10 in Year 1 and $2.30 in Year 2 of the adjustment period.
As an alternative to Brenta increasing dividends, Kovacs proposes a one-time share repurchase using borrowed funds. Kovacs's current EPS forecast for Brenta for the next year is $2.40. The company currently has 3,150,000 shares outstanding, its current share price is $48, and its after-tax cost of borrowing is 3.80%. Kovacs calculates the revised EPS forecast for Brenta, assuming that 300,000 shares are repurchased immediately at the current share price.
Mark Ellis, an analyst, oversees the integration of ESG factors into Valdor's investment analysis. Ellis analyzes current policies and practices related to Brenta's board and recommends changes that would increase governance effectiveness. Brenta's board has 12 members, seven of whom are independent, and is chaired by the company's CEO. The board has audit, compensation, nomination, risk and compliance, and governance committees.

questions.q: The implementation of Kovacs's recommendation regarding Brenta's dividend payout ratio would most likely:
options: increase the agency conflict between Brenta's managers and shareholders.
reduce the agency conflict between Brenta's bondholders and shareholders.
reduce management's ability to invest in negative NPV projects.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. A higher payout reduces, not increases, the manager-shareholder conflict in a mature company.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. A higher payout increases the shareholder-bondholder conflict: dividends reduce the cash cushion for the fixed payments to bondholders.
C. Correct. Correct. A higher payout ratio constrains management's access to capital, so they cannot overinvest in negative NPV projects (manager-shareholder conflict falls).

questions.q: Using a target payout adjustment model, the expected increase in Torvik's dividend per share in Year 2 of the adjustment period is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Increase = (expected earnings × target payout − previous dividend) × adjustment factor. Year 1: (2.10 × 0.60 − 0.40) × 0.20 = $0.172 (dividend $0.572). Year 2: (2.30 × 0.60 − 0.572) × 0.20 = $0.16.
B. Incorrect. This is the Year 1 increase ($0.172), not the Year 2 increase.
C. Incorrect. This uses a 100% target payout instead of 60%: Year 1 (2.10 − 0.40) × 0.20 = 0.34; Year 2 (2.30 − 0.74) × 0.20 = $0.31.

questions.q: If the proposed share repurchase is implemented immediately, Kovacs's revised EPS forecast for Brenta for the next year would be closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. This does not adjust for the new share count: (7,560,000 − 547,200) ÷ 3,150,000 = $2.23.
B. Correct. Earnings = 2.40 × 3,150,000 = 7,560,000; borrowing cost = 3.80% × (48 × 300,000) = 547,200; shares after = 2,850,000; EPS = (7,560,000 − 547,200) ÷ 2,850,000 = $2.46.
C. Incorrect. This ignores the cost of borrowing: 7,560,000 ÷ 2,850,000 = $2.65.

questions.q: Which of the following characteristics of Brenta's board is most likely to pose the greatest potential governance concern?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Seven of the 12 directors (58%) are independent, a majority.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Brenta has the usual set of committees (audit, compensation, nomination, risk and compliance, governance).
C. Correct. Correct. The CEO also chairs the board (CEO duality), which may compromise the board's oversight role.

vignettes.body:
At an international finance and economics conference in Nairobi, Kenya, Mateo Rojas of Chile and Dewi Hartono of Indonesia are discussing how to spur their countries' economic growth. Rojas believes that growth can be bolstered by removing institutional impediments and suggests several possibilities for Chile: clarifying property rights laws, implementing a new dividend tax on foreign investors, and launching a rural literacy program.

Although Hartono recognizes that Indonesia lacks the significant natural resources that Chile has, she states that Indonesia can overcome this challenge by bolstering long-term growth through three channels:

Channel 1: Maintaining a low rupiah exchange rate
Channel 2: Deepening the capital base
Channel 3: Making investments in technology

Kwame Boateng, a fund manager based in Ghana, is concerned about the low standard of living in Ghana and its large informal sector. To improve per capita GDP, Boateng is considering five specific strategies:

Strategy 1: Build daycare centers to increase women's participation in the workforce.
Strategy 2: Impose high tariffs on imports to protect the country's nascent industries.
Strategy 3: Use economic development bank loans to improve the country's transport and manufacturing infrastructure.
Strategy 4: Lower the country's tax rate.
Strategy 5: Introduce policies that encourage the return of highly educated Ghanaian emigrants.

questions.q: Which of Rojas's initiatives is least likely to achieve his stated growth objective?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Education improves human capital and removes an institutional impediment to growth.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Clear property rights remove an institutional impediment and support investment and growth.
C. Correct. Correct. A dividend tax on foreign investors makes equity investment less attractive and impedes capital inflows, which finance domestic investment and growth.

questions.q: The channel that is least likely to help Indonesia overcome its challenge of lacking significant natural resources is:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Investment in technology raises total factor productivity and long-term growth.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Deepening the capital base raises output per worker and potential growth.
C. Correct. Correct. A low exchange rate supports export demand but has little direct effect on the growth of aggregate supply; it is less powerful than capital deepening or technology.

questions.q: The strategy that is least likely to improve per capita GDP in Ghana is:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Correct. With a low standard of living and a large informal sector, the tax rate is unlikely to be the impediment to growth, so lowering it contributes little.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Daycare centers raise labor force participation.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. Returning highly educated emigrants raises human capital.

questions.q: Which of the following strategies being considered by Boateng is most likely to undermine or delay convergence with developed economies?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Infrastructure investment supports growth and convergence.
B. Correct. Correct. High tariffs (trade restrictions) undermine growth: freer trade raises productivity, forces inefficient firms out, allows economies of scale and speeds catch-up through knowledge spillovers.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. Human capital improvements support convergence.

vignettes.body:
Anton Wirth is chief investment officer of ArbiCore Partners (ACP), a multi-asset-class arbitrage hedge fund he recently launched. He has hired Jonas Pell, an analyst with a deep and broad background in security analysis but no experience in arbitrage investing. At their first research meeting, Wirth, who is mentoring Pell, makes the following comments regarding arbitrage using derivative contracts.

Comment 1: The two fundamental rules of arbitrage are that one does not use any of one's own money in a transaction, and one does not take any price risk.
Comment 2: A forward commitment is a derivative instrument in the form of a contract that provides the ability to lock in a price or rate at which one can buy or sell the underlying instrument at some future date or exchange an agreed-on amount of money on a series of dates.
Comment 3: There is a difference between the pricing and the valuation of forward commitments. Pricing involves determining the appropriate forward commitment price or rate, typically after it has been initiated. Valuation involves determining the appropriate rate of the forward commitment when initiating the contract.

Wirth asks Pell to evaluate a carry arbitrage trade for an equity index forward contract. He believes the contract may be mispriced. The index is currently trading at 2,150, and the forward contract expiring in one year is priced at 2,138. The index has a continuously compounded dividend yield of 2.20%, and the one-year continuously compounded interest rate is 0.60%. Wirth believes that at the time of the contract's expiration, the index will be trading at 2,160.

Pell sets out to evaluate arbitrage opportunities using forward rate agreements (FRAs). Wirth makes the following comments to Pell regarding FRAs: "An FRA has two counterparties, a fixed-rate receiver that is short Euribor and a floating-rate receiver that is long Euribor. The party that is long a 2 × 8 FRA must make a Euribor deposit in two months and earns the Euribor rate for the subsequent six months."

Pell also analyzes a US Treasury futures contract that he plans to use to hedge a corporate bond's interest rate risk. He researches the characteristics of Treasury futures and observes the following characteristics.

Characteristic 1: Long and short positions are marked to market each day. Therefore, the contract's market value at the end of each day is zero.
Characteristic 2: Eligible deliverable bonds can have various maturities and coupon rates, and the seller will receive the futures price adjusted by a conversion factor to account for any accrued interest.
Characteristic 3: The underlying deliverable bond in a US Treasury futures contract consists of a basket of bonds from which the short position can deliver the cheapest bond.

questions.q: Which of the comments made by Wirth regarding arbitrage is least likely correct?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Comment 2 defines a forward commitment correctly.
B. Correct. Correct. Comment 3 reverses pricing and valuation: pricing determines the forward price or rate when the contract is initiated; valuation determines its value after initiation.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. Comment 1 states the two arbitrage rules correctly.

questions.q: Does Pell's stock index evaluation most likely identify an arbitrage opportunity?
options: No, the forward is fairly priced
Yes, there is a reverse carry arbitrage opportunity
Yes, there is a carry arbitrage opportunity
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Fair forward price = 2,150 × e^(0.006 − 0.022) = 2,115.87, not 2,138.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Reverse carry applies when the forward is priced below FV(S0), but here the forward is priced above it.
C. Correct. Correct. The forward (2,138) is above the fair price of 2,115.87, so sell the forward, buy the index with borrowed money (carry arbitrage). The expected future index level of 2,160 has no effect on the analysis.

questions.q: Wirth's comments to Pell regarding FRAs are most likely:
options: correct regarding counterparties and correct regarding their transactions.
incorrect regarding counterparties and incorrect regarding their transactions.
correct regarding counterparties and incorrect regarding their transactions.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. The statement that the long party must make a Euribor deposit is wrong.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Wirth describes the counterparties correctly.
C. Correct. Correct. The fixed-rate receiver is short Euribor and the floating-rate receiver is long Euribor, and the timing of a 2 × 8 FRA is described correctly; but an FRA does not require a Euribor deposit (it can be done with one, but it is not required).

questions.q: Which characteristic observed by Pell regarding Treasury futures is least likely correct?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. The short position can deliver the cheapest-to-deliver bond from the basket.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Futures are marked to market daily, so the contract value at the end of each day is zero.
C. Correct. Correct. The conversion factor does not apply to accrued interest: it adjusts each eligible bond to an equivalent bond (for example a 6% coupon bond).

vignettes.body:
Oliver Reeve, an analyst with Corrin Investment Management, is tasked with forecasting future sales for Harlow Tools, a publicly traded retail business specializing in home improvements. Using 25 quarters of sales data ending with the most recent quarter-end date, Reeve estimates a log-linear trend model and creates a forecast of sales for the next four quarters to discuss with his supervisor, Gail Pearce.

Pearce reviews Reeve's forecast and states:

Statement 1) A statistically meaningful low Durbin-Watson statistic indicates that the errors in the model may exhibit positive serial correlation.
Statement 2) If Harlow Tools' sales are growing at a constant rate, a linear trend model may be a better fit than a log-linear model.
Statement 3) As long as the R2 is high, we can be comfortable that the model is a good fit for our analysis.

Next, Pearce asks Reeve to forecast Harlow Tools' net margin (net income/sales) for the next four quarters. Reeve agrees and explains that he will use a first-order autoregressive model since each quarter's net margin appears related to the prior quarter's net margin. Reeve also mentions that he will use an intercept of 0.0380 and a coefficient on the first lag of the net margin of 0.7640.

When applying the first-order autoregressive model, Reeve wants to conduct some tests to ensure the model is producing meaningful results. In order to do this, Reeve comments that he must test whether the:

Test 1: residual autocorrelations differ significantly from 0.
Test 2: intercept and coefficient on the first lag differ significantly from 0.
Test 3: Durbin-Watson statistic differs significantly from 2.

In reviewing the quarterly net margin forecast, Pearce points out that the autocorrelation of the residuals for the 4th lag is significantly different than 0, while lags 1 through 3 are not significantly different than 0, indicating an issue with seasonality. Pearce asks Reeve to build a first-order autoregressive model to forecast earnings per share for the next four quarters, but to account for seasonality in this model.

Reeve reviews the company's earnings per share data and determines that he can create a first-order autoregressive model to account for the seasonality using the information in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1: Seasonal Autoregressive Model Inputs
# Item | Value
Intercept | 0.1980
1 Quarter Lag Coefficient | 0.3720
4 Quarter Lag Coefficient | 0.5430
Earnings Per Share Last Quarter | $2.90
Earnings Per Share 4 Quarters Prior | $2.45

questions.q: Which of Pearce's statements relating to Reeve's forecasted future sales for Harlow Tools is most likely correct?
questions.why:
A. Correct. Correct. A statistically significant low Durbin-Watson statistic indicates that the errors may have positive serial correlation.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. A constant RATE of growth fits a log-linear model; a constant AMOUNT of growth fits a linear trend model.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. A high R2 does not make the model a good fit when the errors are serially correlated.

questions.q: If Harlow Tools' net margin is 12% this quarter, Reeve's first-order autoregressive model will predict the net margin two quarters from now to be closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. This adds the margin to the intercept before multiplying: (0.0380 + 0.12) × 0.7640 = 12.07%.
B. Correct. Apply the model twice: 0.0380 + 0.7640 × 0.12 = 12.97%, then 0.0380 + 0.7640 × 0.1297 = 13.71%.
C. Incorrect. This adds the intercept twice: 0.0380 + 0.0380 + 0.7640 × 0.12 = 16.77%.

questions.q: Of the three tests Reeve indicates he would like to conduct for the first-order autoregressive model, which is most likely appropriate to test for serial correlation in the model?
questions.why:
A. Correct. Correct. Serial correlation in an autoregressive model is tested through the residual autocorrelations (t-tests of each lag).
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. The Durbin-Watson statistic cannot be used when a lagged dependent variable is an independent variable.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. This tests the coefficients, not the residuals.

questions.q: Once adjusted for seasonality, based on data in Exhibit 1, the forecasted earnings per share for the current quarter is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. This leaves out the intercept: 0.3720 × 2.90 + 0.5430 × 2.45 = $2.41.
B. Correct. 0.1980 + 0.3720 × 2.90 + 0.5430 × 2.45 = $2.61.
C. Incorrect. This matches the coefficients with the wrong lags: 0.1980 + 0.3720 × 2.45 + 0.5430 × 2.90 = $2.68.

vignettes.body:
Anders Lund, CFA, is an equity analyst with Northgate Securities. Lund is preparing a research report on Rennes Industrie, SA, a publicly traded company based in France that complies with IFRS 9. As part of his analysis, Lund has assembled data gathered from the financial statement footnotes of Rennes's 2018 Annual Report and from discussions with company management. Lund is concerned about the effect of this information on Rennes's future earnings.

Information about Rennes's investment portfolio for the years ended 31 December 2017 and 2018 is presented in Exhibit 1. As part of his research, Lund is considering the possible effect on reported income of Rennes's accounting classification for fixed income investments.

Exhibit 1: Rennes's Investment Portfolio (€ Thousands)
# Characteristic | Alder AG | Brookes Corp | Corvin SA
Classification | FVPL | FVOCI | Amortized cost
Cost* | €30,000 | €45,000 | €60,000
Market value, 31 December 2017 | 33,000 | 43,000 | 64,500
Market value, 31 December 2018 | 31,500 | 41,500 | 66,000
Note: * All securities were acquired at par value.

In addition, Rennes's annual report discusses a transaction under which receivables were securitized through a special purpose entity (SPE) for Rennes's benefit.

questions.q: The balance sheet carrying value of Rennes's investment portfolio (in € thousands) at 31 December 2018 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Under IFRS 9, FVPL and FVOCI securities are carried at market value and amortized cost securities at historical cost: 31,500 + 41,500 + 60,000 = €133,000.
B. Incorrect. This carries all three securities at cost: 30,000 + 45,000 + 60,000 = 135,000.
C. Incorrect. This carries all three securities at 2018 market value: 31,500 + 41,500 + 66,000 = 139,000.

questions.q: Compared to Rennes's reported earnings before taxes in 2018, if Corvin had been classified as a FVPL security, the earnings before taxes (in € thousands) would have been:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. There was an unrealized gain, not a loss, so earnings would be higher.
B. Correct. Correct. Unrealized gains and losses are included in income for FVPL securities: during 2018 Corvin's market value rose from 64,500 to 66,000, a gain of €1,500.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. FVPL classification brings the unrealized gain or loss into income, so earnings would change.

questions.q: Rennes's reported interest income would be lower if the cost was the same but the par value (in € thousands) of:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Par above cost means a discount, which is amortized upward: interest income would be higher.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Par above cost means a discount: interest income would be higher.
C. Correct. Correct. Par (41,500) below the cost (45,000) means a premium; amortizing the premium under the effective interest method makes interest income lower than the coupon received.

questions.q: Rennes's special purpose entity is most likely to be:
options: consolidated on Rennes's financial statements only if it is a "qualifying SPE."
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Qualifying SPEs existed only under US GAAP (now eliminated); IFRS does not allow that classification.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Under IFRS the SPE is not kept off-balance sheet.
C. Correct. Correct. Under IFRS, SPEs conducted for the benefit of the sponsoring entity must be consolidated; IFRS has no qualifying SPE.

vignettes.body:
Choi Min-jun and Sandra Lee, junior analysts at Seoul Capital, are valuing Eldor Telecom (Eldor), a regional telecom provider. Their supervisor instructed them to use residual income models for the valuation.

Lee starts the meeting by saying she wants to be sure Choi understands the difference between the residual income approach and the dividend discount approach and makes the following statements:

Statement 1: The residual income model has more of its value determined in the current time period, whereas the dividend discount model has more of its value determined in later periods.
Statement 2: The residual income model makes assumptions about future earnings and dividend growth, whereas the dividend discount model makes assumptions only about dividend growth.
Statement 3: If there is clean surplus accounting, the residual income model and the dividend discount model will yield the same results.
To start their analysis, the analysts gather the information in Exhibit 1 for Eldor and calculate the forecasted residual income for the current fiscal year ending 30 June.

Exhibit 1: Forecasted Residual Income
# Item | Per share
Book value per share 30 June previous year | $44.00
Forecasted earnings for year-end 30 June current year | $6.90
Book value per share 30 June current fiscal year | $49.10
Required rate of return = re | 12%
Long-term growth rate | 5%
Return on equity (ROE) | 14%

They continue by selecting the single-stage residual income model to calculate the intrinsic value of Eldor.

Next, the analysts decide to calculate the economic value added (EVA) for Eldor and gather some additional data (Exhibit 2):

Exhibit 2: Eldor Telecom Additional Information (US$, thousands)
# Item | Value
Total debt, 30 June previous fiscal year | $3,850,000
Total equity, 30 June previous fiscal year | $1,960,000
Earnings before interest and taxes | $580,000
Tax rate | 25%
Weighted average cost of capital (WACC) | 6.5%

questions.q: In Lee's comparison of the residual income and dividend discount models, which of her statements is least accurate?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. With clean surplus accounting the two models give the same results: this statement is accurate.
B. Correct. Correct. The residual income model does NOT make separate assumptions about future earnings and dividend growth, so this statement is the least accurate.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. The residual income model recognizes more of the value in the current period (book value): this statement is accurate.

questions.q: Using Exhibit 1, the forecasted residual income per share for the current fiscal year is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. This uses the ending book value: 6.90 − 0.12 × 49.10 = $1.01.
B. Correct. RI = EPS − equity charge on beginning book value = 6.90 − 0.12 × 44.00 = $1.62.
C. Incorrect. This is only the equity charge: 0.12 × 44.00 = $5.28.

questions.q: Using Exhibit 1 and the single-stage residual income model, the intrinsic value of Eldor is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. V0 = B0 + B0 × (ROE − r) ÷ (r − g) = 44.00 + 44.00 × (0.14 − 0.12) ÷ (0.12 − 0.05) = $56.57.
B. Incorrect. This capitalizes the forecast residual income of $1.62 instead of the ROE-based residual income: 44.00 + 1.62 ÷ (0.12 − 0.05) = $67.14.
C. Incorrect. This subtracts g instead of r in the numerator: 44.00 + 44.00 × (0.14 − 0.05) ÷ (0.12 − 0.05) = $100.57.

questions.q: Using Exhibit 2, the EVA for Eldor is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. NOPAT = 580,000 × 0.75 = 435,000; total capital = 3,850,000 + 1,960,000 = 5,810,000; EVA = 435,000 − 6.5% × 5,810,000 = $57,350.
B. Incorrect. This uses pre-tax EBIT: 580,000 − 6.5% × 5,810,000 = $202,350.
C. Incorrect. This is NOPAT only, with no capital charge.

vignettes.body:
Katrin Aalto is a portfolio manager in the fixed-income division of Sierra Wealth Management (SWM), based in Denver. Aalto is running a training session for newly hired analysts Diego Ramos, Ivan Petrov, and Arun Mehta to examine the use of Credit Default Swaps (CDSs) in fixed-income portfolio management.

Aalto notes that a payment from the credit protection seller to the credit protection buyer is triggered whenever a credit event occurs. She asks each of the analysts to identify a credit event in the United States that will trigger a payment. The following are the responses of each analyst:

Ramos: "If the reference entity fails to make a scheduled interest or principal payment, it is recognized as a failure-to-pay credit event."
Petrov: "A change in seniority of outstanding obligations is also recognized as a credit event that will trigger a payment by the protection seller."
Mehta: "A declaration of bankruptcy by the reference entity is a credit event that will trigger a payment from the CDS seller."
To facilitate a discussion of CDS pricing and CDS trading strategies, Aalto presents the group with the information in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1: Select CDS Information
# CDS | Type | Credit Spread (bps) | Tenor (yrs.) | Coupon (bps) | Duration
CDX NA IG | Index | 62 | 5 | 100 | 4.71
CDX NA HY | Index | 355 | 5 | 500 | 4.30
Company A | Single-Name | 207 | 5 | 100 | 4.52
Company A | Single-Name | 281 | 10 | 100 | 7.31
Company B | Single-Name | 172 | 5 | 500 | 4.50
Company B | Single-Name | 338 | 10 | 500 | 8.05
Note: CDX NA IG is an index of CDSs of investment-grade North American corporations. CDX NA HY is an index of CDSs of high-yield North American corporations.

Aalto states, "I would like you to formulate appropriate CDS trading strategies using the information provided in the following statements:"

Statement 1: "Our economists expect the US economy to weaken over the coming year, with spreads on high-yield CDSs widening by 150 bps and spreads on investment-grade CDSs widening by 10 bps."
Statement 2: "Our analysts expect that the credit curve for Company A will steepen, whereas the credit curve for Company B is expected to flatten."
Only Mehta responds, as follows: "A trade that addresses Statement 2 would be to buy Company A CDSs with a 10-year tenor and sell Company A CDSs with a 5-year tenor. Alternatively, one could buy Company B CDSs with a 10-year tenor and sell Company B CDSs with a 5-year tenor."

questions.q: With regard to Aalto's question on credit events, who is least likely correct?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Bankruptcy is a credit event in the United States and elsewhere.
B. Correct. Correct. In the United States a restructuring (a change in seniority of obligations) is not recognized as a credit event that triggers a payment; it is recognized outside the United States.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. Failure to pay is a credit event in the United States and elsewhere.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the price per 100 par of Company A 5-year CDSs is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Upfront premium = (credit spread − coupon) × duration = (2.07% − 1.00%) × 4.52 = 4.84; price = 100 − 4.84 = 95.16.
B. Incorrect. This leaves out the duration: 100 − (2.07 − 1.00) = 98.93.
C. Incorrect. This reverses the sign of the spread difference: 100 − (1.00 − 2.07) × 4.52 = 104.84.

questions.q: Based on the information in Exhibit 1 and Statement 1, an appropriate long/short trade would be to:
options: buy CDX NA HY and sell CDX NA IG.
sell Company B CDSs and buy Company A CDSs.
sell CDX NA HY and buy CDX NA IG.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Correct. The economy is expected to weaken, so spreads widen: high-yield spreads (+150 bps) widen by more than investment-grade spreads (+10 bps). Buying CDX NA HY protection gains more than the loss on the sold CDX NA IG.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Company B (500 bps coupon) is high yield and Company A (100 bps) is investment grade; selling B protection and buying A protection loses when spreads widen.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. Selling HY protection and buying IG protection is appropriate when the economy is expected to strengthen.

questions.q: Is Mehta's response to Statement 2 by Aalto most likely correct?
options: No, he is incorrect about the trade involving Company A CDSs.
No, he is incorrect about the trade involving Company B CDSs.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Only the Company A trade is correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. For Company A (steepening) the right trade is to buy the 10-year and sell the 5-year CDS, which is exactly what Mehta says.
C. Correct. Correct. Company B's curve is expected to flatten, so the appropriate trade is to sell the long-term (10-year) CDS and buy the short-term (5-year) CDS. Mehta proposes the opposite for Company B.

vignettes.body:
Daniel Frost and Priya Nair, interns in the financial institutions division of an investment firm, are cleaning up outstanding issues in a few files.

They start by examining the investment allocation and returns on the investment portfolio for Corvus Life Group, a life and health insurance company, using data Frost prepared (Exhibit 1).

Exhibit 1: Investment Allocation and Returns, Corvus Life Group, in $ Millions
# Investment portfolio as of 31 December | 2018 | 2017
Loans and deposits | 7,900 | 8,300
Debt securities | 128,500 | 120,200
Equity securities | 36,400 | 30,900
# Investment returns for the year ending 31 December | 2018 | 2017
Interest income | 5,980 | 5,420
Gains (losses) on fixed-income investments | 410 | (95)

Frost asks, "Why does Corvus have a much larger portion of its investment portfolio in equity securities compared with the property and casualty company we were working on yesterday?"

Nair replies, "Corvus can take greater risks with its investments for two reasons: First, its claims have a shorter duration, and second, its claims are relatively more predictable."

Next, they turn their attention to a commercial bank file that still required some work on the assessment of earnings quality, using summary earnings information prepared by Nair (Exhibit 2).

Exhibit 2: Selected Earnings Information from Bank File, in $ Thousands
# Item | 2018 | 2017 | 2016 | 2015 | 2014
Interest income | 598,200 | 575,500 | 568,000 | 569,400 | 561,000
Interest expense | 212,000 | 217,300 | 231,100 | 244,800 | 246,200
Net interest income | 386,200 | 358,200 | 336,900 | 324,600 | 314,800
Trading income | 2,900 | 4,700 | 6,100 | (800) | 14,200
Other income | 126,300 | 117,600 | 109,800 | 110,900 | 93,900
Total income net of interest expense | 515,400 | 480,500 | 452,800 | 434,700 | 422,900
Provision for credit losses | 7,900 | 12,600 | 9,300 | 9,700 | 6,600
Earnings before taxes | 108,900 | 89,400 | 85,700 | 74,100 | 81,300

Nair states, "We have to finish the CAMELS (capital adequacy, asset quality, management capabilities, earnings sufficiency, liquidity position, and sensitivity to market risk) analysis on this file. In my preliminary review of the bank's earnings information, I assigned a score reflecting high quality of earnings, based on the following points:

Point 1: The proportion of total income from net interest income has been stable in the most recent years.
Point 2: Net interest income has been growing at a constant rate over the period.
Point 3: The trading income is volatile, but it is a small portion of the earnings."

Frost replies, "I think we need to dig a little deeper. We need to look at the estimates that are used to determine earnings and whether the bank is using them to manage earnings before taxes (EBT). The provision for credit losses is an estimate where management can exercise wide discretion. Let's look at what portion of the 2018 increase in EBT comes from the change in that estimate."

questions.q: The average return on fixed-income assets for Corvus in 2018 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. This leaves out the gains on fixed-income investments: 5,980 ÷ 132,450 = 4.5%.
B. Correct. Return = (interest income + gains on fixed-income investments) ÷ average fixed-income assets = (5,980 + 410) ÷ [½ (7,900 + 128,500) + ½ (8,300 + 120,200)] = 6,390 ÷ 132,450 = 4.8%.
C. Incorrect. This leaves out loans and deposits from fixed-income assets: 6,390 ÷ 124,350 = 5.1%.

questions.q: Nair's reply to Frost's question concerning the higher portion of equity securities in Corvus's investment portfolio is best described as correct with respect to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. The first reason (shorter duration) is wrong; the second reason is the correct one.
B. Correct. Correct. Corvus is a life and health insurer: its claims are more predictable and have a longer duration than P&C claims. Only the predictability reason is stated correctly.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. The claims of a life and health insurer have a LONGER duration than those of a P&C company, so the first reason is wrong.

questions.q: Using Exhibit 2, which of Nair's points in support of the CAMELS score she assigns for earnings quality is least accurate? The point concerning:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Trading income is volatile but a small portion of income (about 0.6% in 2018): this supports earnings quality.
B. Correct. Correct. Net interest income growth has been rising (3.1%, 3.8%, 6.3%, 7.8%), not constant.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. Net interest income is about 74-75% of total income net of interest expense in each year: stable, which supports earnings quality.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 2, the proportion of the increase in the 2018 earnings before taxes that comes from the change in the provision for credit losses is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. This is the change in the provision (4,700) divided by 2018 EBT: 4,700 ÷ 108,900 = 4.3%.
B. Incorrect. This is the provision as a proportion of 2018 EBT, ignoring changes: 7,900 ÷ 108,900 = 7.3%.
C. Correct. EBT rose by 108,900 − 89,400 = 19,500 while the provision fell by 12,600 − 7,900 = 4,700: 4,700 ÷ 19,500 = 24.1%.

vignettes.body:
Corinne Valeri is the new chief investment officer at Public Educators Retirement Fund (PERF), which oversees 18 funds from 9 different firms. She plans to implement new performance measurement tools for selecting and evaluating PERF's managers.

Valeri is meeting with her staff to gauge what they know about manager selection and evaluation. She starts by asking her staff to share with her their understanding of the term "value added." She notes the following responses from three analysts, Owen Brandt, Lena Sorg, and Tara Quill.

Quill: Value added can come from multiple sources, including asset allocation and security selection.
Brandt: A manager adds value when the portfolio return is greater than that of its benchmark.
Sorg: A manager adds value when he produces a positive rate of return.
Valeri reviews data compiled by Brandt for Danube Investment Advisers for the meeting. After reviewing Brandt's work, Valeri requests that the analysts include the information ratio in all future exhibits.

Exhibit 1: Danube Investment Advisers: Selected Statistics
# Item | Value
Fund average annual return (%) | 17.62
Fund standard deviation | 11.4
Benchmark average annual return (%) | 17.05
Benchmark standard deviation | 10.1
Active risk | 1.90

Because the analysts are unfamiliar with the use of the information ratio, Valeri explains how it might be useful in investment manager selection and in choosing the level of active portfolio risk. She asks each analyst to make an observation about his or her understanding of the information ratio.

Sorg: The information ratio appears to be the best criterion to evaluate the past performance of our active managers.
Quill: The information ratio will change as the active weights deviate from the benchmark weights.
Brandt: Because PERF's investment policy prohibits short positions, PERF would be unable to take advantage of any optimized portfolios with increased active risk.
Valeri points out that the Sharpe ratio and the information ratio are both useful tools in evaluating portfolio managers and asks Brandt to explain some of the important differences between the two.

Brandt notes, "The information ratio is a measure of relative expected or realized reward to risk, whereas the Sharpe ratio measures the absolute risk–return trade-off of a portfolio. Sharpe ratios help investors focus on the relative value added by active management. Although the information ratio is not affected by the addition of cash or leverage, the Sharpe ratio is affected by the addition of either."

questions.q: Which statement regarding the measurement of value added is least likely to be correct?
questions.why:
A. Correct. Correct. A positive return alone is not value added; value added is the portfolio return minus the benchmark return (RA = RP − RB).
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Value added can come from several sources, including asset allocation and security selection: this statement is correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. Value added is the portfolio return above the benchmark return: this statement is correct.

questions.q: Based on the information presented in Exhibit 1, the information ratio for Danube is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. This divides the active return by the benchmark standard deviation: 0.57 ÷ 10.1 = 0.06.
B. Correct. IR = active return ÷ active risk = (17.62 − 17.05) ÷ 1.90 = 0.30.
C. Incorrect. This uses the difference in standard deviations as active risk: 0.57 ÷ (11.4 − 10.1) = 0.44.

questions.q: With respect to the information ratio, which analyst's observation is least likely correct?
questions.why:
A. Correct. Correct. The information ratio is unaffected by the aggressiveness of the active weights, because active return and active risk rise proportionally.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. To increase active risk one would need to short the benchmark (short positions), so Brandt's statement is correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. The information ratio is the best criterion to evaluate past performance of active managers: correct.

questions.q: In his statement regarding the information and Sharpe ratios, Brandt is most likely correct with regard to:
options: the impact of cash and leverage.
the Sharpe ratio and relative value.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. The Sharpe ratio is unaffected by cash or leverage, while the information ratio is affected.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. It is the information ratio, not the Sharpe ratio, that focuses on relative value added.
C. Correct. Correct. The information ratio measures relative reward to risk; the Sharpe ratio measures the absolute risk-return trade-off.

vignettes.body:
Jacob Kostecka, CFA, is a portfolio manager at Forkson Investment Management, an asset management and research focused organization. After obtaining his CFA charter last month, Kostecka was transferred to the private wealth management division at Forkson.

Dharshi Bope, a private wealth client, was involved in a major motorcycle accident and is in critical condition, fighting for his life. Bope is a single parent with a daughter, Paveen Nathoo, in her mid-twenties. Since the accident, Nathoo has managed her father’s affairs, paying all expenses, including investment advisory fees. In several conversations with Nathoo, Kostecka highlighted Bope’s low risk tolerance and investment goal of capital preservation. Nathoo has indicated her interest in managing the account more aggressively and possibly moving to another management firm. Nathoo recently petitioned the court to appoint her full power of attorney to legally manage Bope’s affairs. Prior to the court decision, Nathoo asks Kostecka to invest her father’s account in the initial public offering (IPO) of Chatterbox, a highly sought after social media company that has yet to generate a profit.

The following week, the court approves Nathoo’s request to act on behalf of her father.

Nathoo establishes a non-discretionary investment account at Forkson tied to her newly established business. Shortly thereafter, Kostecka joins the board of Jabbertalk.com, a smaller social media competitor to Chatterbox. Based on his knowledge of Chatterbox, Kostecka believes the stock of Jabbertalk is a good investment, even though it is not yet profitable. Buoyed by his faith in social media, Kostecka ultimately purchases shares of Jabbertalk’s IPO for Nathoo’s account, as well as for all clients he currently manages. When Kostecka informs Nathoo of the purchase, she expresses concern about her legal responsibilities and lack of accounting knowledge in overseeing the account. Kostecka provides Nathoo a list of recommended professionals he has worked with in the past, including attorneys and accountants. When he was in college 10 years earlier, Kostecka was engaged to one of the attorneys but broke off the relationship prior to their wedding, and one of the accountants was Kostecka’s college roommate. Since then, Kostecka has not had any contact with the lawyer and accountant.

The Jabbertalk investment is profitable on the first day of trading, doubling from its opening price. Kostecka tells his clients the multifactor valuation model used by Forkson shows Jabbertalk stock is still undervalued. Forkson’s research report, due out the next day, will recommend investors hold their Jabbertalk shares. However, Kostecka tells all his clients simultaneously they should sell their shares because he believes Jabbertalk is overvalued and the stock price will fall soon. Kostecka notes he has followed through on this belief by selling his personal holdings of Jabbertalk shares. Nathoo ignores Kostecka’s recommendation to sell Jabbertalk. Over the next week, the stock declines 75%.

Watching Jabbertalk’s severe share price decline, Nathoo becomes furious with Kostecka because he did not sell shares of Jabbertalk in her account. She files a complaint with Kostecka’s supervisor, Sally Fang, CFA, claiming she was misled on the value of the IPO in the days immediately after the stock started trading. Kostecka responds to the complaint by telling Fang, “the analyst who wrote the hold recommendation on Jabbertalk has only passed his CFA Level II examination. As a charterholder, I have earned the right to use the CFA designation, so I am more qualified to manage clients’ investments.”

questions.q: With regard to the investment request made by Nathoo to invest in Chatterbox, Kostecka should most likely:
questions.why: The account should be managed according to the client’s investment goal of capital preservation and a low risk tolerance. Under Standard III(A) –Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, the first step for members and candidates in fulfilling their duty of loyalty to clients is to determine the identity of the “client” to whom the duty of loyalty is owed.

questions.q: With regard to investing in Jabbertalk and recommending experts, Kostecka most likely needs to disclose conflicts related to his:
questions.why: Kostecka’s board service creates the opportunity to receive material nonpublic information involving Jabbertalk and is a basic conflict of interest. As a result, according to Standard VI(A)–Conflicts of Interest, the directorship should be disclosed.

questions.q: In relation to Kostecka’s handling of the Jabbertalk stock recommendation, which of the following CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct did he least likely violate?
questions.why: Standard III(B)–Fair Dealing requires members and candidates to deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities.

questions.q: When Kostecka defends himself against Nathoo’s complaint, he most likely violated the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct concerning the:
options: reference to candidacy in the CFA Program.
right to use the CFA designation.
misrepresentation of the meaning of the designation.
questions.why: Statements overstating the competency of an individual or imply, either directly or indirectly, that superior performance can be expected from someone with the CFA designation are not allowed under Standard VII(B)–Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program.
